skyline.text: How a law against homosexuality became a police extortion racket
Why India must spend its scarce state capability on basics
A codebreaker’s life destroyed by state coercion over private matters

footnote.text: I haven’t paid the hafta to the state.

brief.head: Safer than sugar
brief.text: Marijuana is less harmful than alcohol or cigarettes and far less harmful than sugar, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah wants drugs treated as a public-health issue, not a crime. {073-C08}

brief.head: The best option open
brief.text: India’s law defines prostitution as exploitation or abuse, Amit Varma said, leaving consent out. Anyone who chooses sex work, he argued, has picked the best option open to them. {073-C09}

brief.head: Punished for failing
brief.text: When Amit Varma was growing up, suicide was illegal in India: “the one crime for which you got punished if you failed to commit it.” {073-J01}

brief.head: When winning loses
brief.text: A high black-market price shows a ban is being enforced, Ajay Shah said, but it also tells criminals there is money to be made. {073-C04}

brief.head: Crime, incorporated
brief.text: Bans let crime scale up from lone rangers into firms, Ajay Shah said. Import barriers bred smuggling, and smuggling built Haji Mastan’s gangs. {073-C05}

thought.who: Amit Varma, arguing that betting done in the open can be watched and regulated

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what the law should punish
lead.head: No victim, no crime
body: Someone wrote in after an earlier episode with a question: what is a victimless crime? Doesn’t every crime have a victim?

Amit Varma’s answer, over the next hour, was that the phrase is a misnomer. A crime, he said, infringes someone’s rights: killing them, or stealing their property. Acts that harm no one are not crimes at all. “If there is a crime, there must be a victim.” {073-C01}
Being illegal, he argued, is not the same as being wrong. Most such laws come from a wish not merely to protect rights but to “engineer society to our wishes”.
Varma, with Ajay Shah asking the questions, took the idea through alcohol, drugs, gambling, prostitution, homosexuality, suicide and hate speech.
## Three objections

His case rested on three objections. The first is moral: consenting adults should be free to associate with each other as they please, “whether it is in the bedroom, the marketplace, or the public square”.
The second is practical. A ban does not end demand: the underworld springs up, coercion and fraud come in, and the desired outcome never arrives.

The third is about power. Whoever holds the state’s monopoly on coercion will use it to remake society to their own values. “The person you hate most in the world could be in power tomorrow,” Varma warned, “and they’ll pass laws according to their values.” {073-C02}

Prohibition was the clearest case. Drawing on the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle, Varma described two apparent enemies: the Baptist, who demands a ban on moral grounds, and the bootlegger, who profits from it.
“The Baptist wants alcohol banned, so he can do his virtue signaling,” he said, “and the bootlegger wants alcohol banned so he can make money on the black market.” {073-C03}
Wherever the state bans something, the police also find leverage. Varma’s starkest example was the Matunga racket, in which Bombay police posed as men looking for love to trap and extort gay men.
## Instinct and reason
Not every case was simple. Varma told of a German cannibal whose victim consented on camera, and of thought experiments that instinct condemns but reason cannot fault.
Moral instincts, he said, come from prehistoric programming nobody fully understands. When the powerful want to outlaw something because it feels wrong, that is all the more reason for suspicion.
Shah added that even the richest states execute innocent people, and India has very little state capability to spare.
## Means and ends

If the worry is wives beaten by drunk husbands, Shah argued, banning alcohol is the wrong lever. The right one is easy no-fault divorce, with jointly created wealth split equally, so that an abused spouse can walk away.
“So just an emotional outrage is the surest way of getting to a wrong answer,” he said. {073-C15}
Growth, Shah added, is the greatest instrument for the emancipation of women. Varma extended that to every marginalised group.

Shah closed with Alan Turing, whose life was destroyed by British laws on homosexuality. The mainstream was once completely wrong about homosexuality and divorce, he said, and getting the state out worked.
Once you accept that, Shah said, you should doubt the rest of conventional wisdom on state power, drug laws included. {073-C17}
Varma’s last word was a principle: the coercive power of the state should never get in the way of individuals, “even if you regard their actions as unethical”.

second.label: Criminal justice
second.head: The state’s fatal errors
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the death penalty, and what it says about state power
body: Roughly 5 per cent of people executed by the state in advanced economies are later believed to have been innocent, Ajay Shah said. These are countries with the best state capability in the world, whose judges demand the highest level of evidence. {073-C13}

“Under Indian conditions,” he asked, “what do you think is the fail rate of the state?” He had no estimates, but large numbers of innocent people, he said, are put into the slammer by the Indian state. {#slammer}
Every conviction, Shah argued, deserves scepticism, and so does any plan to turn such a flawed instrument on people’s private choices.

quote.text: One in twenty is actually innocent, and the state went and caught the wrong guy or did some horrible things.

second.caption: the death penalty’s error rate

third.head: Beautiful intent, bad law
body: At a literary festival recently, Amit Varma shared a stage with an MP who had brought a bill against hate speech on platforms. “I get the intent,” Varma told him. “It’s very beautiful.” {073-S06}

Then came the warning, from twenty-five years of writing about free speech: “Laws against hate speech will always be used against free speech.” Always and everywhere, he said, the state uses such laws to attack dissenters. {073-C11}
Varma, a free speech absolutist, draws the line at direct incitement to harm: telling someone to go and beat Amit is wrong because the beating is a crime.
Laws such as 295A and 153A sound well meant, but can be read to lock up anyone. Hate speech is bad, he said, but power over it will be turned on “people like us”.
third.caption: the MP and the hate-speech bill

p2.title: Mind your own business
p2.deck: Amit Varma takes his case against punishing victimless crimes through alcohol, gambling and the limits of the state

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Illegal, but not wrong
sections.caption: the line between illegal and wrong
body: In the popular imagination, Amit Varma said, breaking the law is a crime. That is legally correct. The larger question is what the law should consider a crime, and whatever is illegal is not necessarily wrong. {#illegal}

His own test is a liberal one. All of us have rights, and they hold only as far as they do not infringe the rights of others. Murder infringes the right to life, theft the right to property, and the whole purpose of the state is to stop such infringements.
Victimless crimes harm no one else. The state outlaws them anyway, he argued, because it wants to remake society, tweaking laws “like an engineer does” until it gets the outcomes it desires.
## The case against bans

The first of his objections is moral: when the state interferes with voluntary interactions that harm no one else, “everything goes to hell”. The second is practical: a ban does not end demand, so the underworld comes in and things get worse.

The third is about power. The state needs a monopoly on coercion to protect rights, Varma said, but it exists to serve us, not the other way round. Give it power to refashion society, and whoever holds it next will pass laws according to their own values. {073-C02}
~ Homosexuality, effectively illegal in India until recently, showed the cost. Those were “the mores of an earlier, darker time”, he said, and they destroyed lives.

quote.text: We should not automatically assume that whatever is illegal is necessarily wrong from an ethical perspective

sections.label: Alcohol
sections.head: The pulpit and the still
sections.caption: Baptists and bootleggers
body: Prohibition, Amit Varma said, has never worked anywhere in human history. He has had alcohol in Gujarat, and in Lahore, where despite prohibition there was a flourishing black market. {073-S04}

He borrowed a frame from the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle. A Baptist gives moral grounds for a ban; then a bootlegger supplies lower-quality, unregulated alcohol, and stories of hooch poisoning follow. {#hooch}
That is why, Varma said, the film *Raees* got it completely wrong by setting Shah Rukh Khan’s bootlegger against a goody-goody anti-alcohol politician. Their incentives are exactly aligned. {073-C03}
## The price of success

Ajay Shah added a twist. Successful enforcement shows up as a high black-market price, and high prices draw criminals in. “If you try to go after this and you even succeed in the short term, you’re only stoking greater effort and greater organizational capacity in the long run.” {073-C04}

Import duties, Varma said, punish a victimless crime too: “I buy something in America, I bring it here, and I sell it to a friend. And immediately it is a crime because I haven’t paid the hafta to the state.” {073-J05}

~ Where the state bans something, he added, badly paid police collect hafta from the underworld and from ordinary offenders. He called people in law enforcement excellent people. “But the incentives are what they are.”

quote.text: I might not partake of them, but other people have agency, and if they wish to do so, that’s the way it is.

sections.label: Gambling
sections.head: All of life is a bet
sections.caption: why we are all gamblers
body: Amit Varma was a professional poker player for five years. {#fiveyears} His first point about gambling was that everyone gambles.

Talking to a girl in a bar, marrying, choosing a job, buying a house or investing in stocks: each is a bet on an intuitive sense of probabilities. Even putting Pi on Ajay Shah’s lap during the shoot was a gamble, weighing the risk of disruption against “the oxytocin flooding through you”. {073-J03}
If gambling means weighing probabilities and betting on your best judgment, Varma said, then everything is gambling, and singling out some forms for stigma makes no sense. {073-C07}
## Out of the shadows

Varma was a cricket journalist for many years, when match-fixing was a scourge. People conflate betting and match-fixing, he said, but match-fixing happens because betting is illegal: the underworld runs it, and nobody looks at its money flows.

Imagine instead, he said, that HDFC or IDFC offered gambling accounts, much as a demat account holds shares, with light-touch regulation against fraud and match-fixing. Everything would be in the open. “Sunlight is the best disinfectant.” {073-C06}
~ Players are paid much more today, he noted, so the incentives for fixing have changed. But the shady dealing happens wherever the underworld is.

quote.text: Everything we do is gambling and we should not necessarily stigmatise certain forms of gambling.

sections.label: State capability
sections.head: Few jobs, done well
sections.caption: the limits of state capability
body: Ajay Shah, drawing on his work with Vijay Kelkar, treats state capability as a finite budget. India, a poor country, has very little of it. {073-C14}

Rich countries such as Sweden or the UK can afford to splurge it. India, Shah said, has “a teensy-weensy amount of state capability” and should spend it on a few primordial, important problems. {073-J10}
Defence, monetary policy, criminal justice, financial regulation and a tax system: learning these basics, he said, is a journey of fifty or a hundred years. {#fiftyhundred}
## First things first

Amit Varma agreed, and went further. The Indian state does too many things badly, he said, and victimless crimes should not be on its list at all. Except for the privileged, the rule of law does not exist in India. “Get that right first.”

For wives beaten by drunk husbands, Shah’s remedy is not prohibition but easy, frictionless no-fault divorce, with jointly created wealth split equally, giving an abused spouse the power to walk away. {073-C15}

~ Varma reads rising divorce rates as a sign of women’s empowerment. He recalled a Twitter rant listing five things Ronald Reagan got wrong, “and as I was reading through them I realized that he got all of them right.” One was no-fault divorce. {073-J09}

quote.text: When you have very little capability, the wise thing to do is to focus that capability on a few primordial and important problems

sections.label: The last word
sections.head: Fan the spark of doubt
sections.caption: Alan Turing and the spark of doubt
body: Ajay Shah’s recommendation was a person and a story: Alan Turing. He played a critical part in cracking the German Enigma machines, Shah said, and was the first theoretical computer scientist. {#turing}
Turing’s life was destroyed because he fell afoul of old British laws about homosexuality. Study it, Shah said, and “it will reshape your moral calculus”.

For Amit Varma, Turing’s is the story of all homosexuals for most of human history. In India, he said, those who had to hide lived Thoreau’s “lives of quiet desperation”, made worse because they could not even express their sexuality. {073-J12}
## Where doubt leads
Shah sees decriminalised homosexuality and no-fault divorce as the first stirrings of liberal values: places where people woke up, said “How dare you?” and got the government out, with great success.
Once you accept that mainstream thinking was completely wrong on these questions, he said, you should question the rest, including the use of state power on drugs. {073-C17}
~ Varma’s principle is to get the state out first. Once that is done, he said, society hopefully evolves.

quote.text: We owe it to ourselves to blow oxygen on the spark of doubt in our hearts

side.boxText: All of modern liberalism, Amit Varma said, emanates from John Locke’s idea of self-ownership. “I am my own property, I own myself.” The rights to life, free speech and property all flow from that. {#locke}

contQuote.text: If someone has chosen to be a prostitute, they have done so because it is the best option open to them and now it is up to you to contemplate how bad the other options must be.

p3.title: The case files
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts told, and what each says about bans

stories.start: So many years ago our our friend Vikram Doctor had pointed me
stories.end: because three seventy is gone, the Matunga racket is not possible anymore
stories.caption: the Matunga racket
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what a ban on love gave Bombay’s police
stories.head: Coffee at Matunga, cash at the ATM
body: Around 2007 and 2008, before dating apps, gay men in Bombay found each other through classified websites, where people posted that they were looking for a lover or for friendship. {#matunga2007}

Amit Varma’s friend Vikram Doctor told him about a scheme the police were running. {073-R12} A policeman would advertise on such a site, posing as someone looking for love, and suggest meeting at Matunga station for coffee and a chat.
When the man arrived, the cops nabbed him. Then they extorted money, threatening to tell his parents or his wife.
Sometimes, Doctor told Varma, they took the man inside an ATM and emptied his account. {#atm}
The man could do nothing. He had been made to feel what Varma called “almost a primal shame”, a shame constructed by society and the state and then used to extort money from him.

Varma wrote about it in a column in *Mint*, and he does not blame a few rotten policemen. “To me this is not a bunch of bad cops,” he said. “To me this is the incentives, this is the nature of the state.” {073-S01}
Why outlaw something that is natural, voluntary and infringes no one’s rights? Once the law went, he said, the Matunga racket was no longer possible.
~ The same thing can happen in any context. In a state with prohibition, Varma said, police can raid your house, find half a bottle of whiskey and drag you away, and that is monstrous.
stories.why: Outlaw a victimless act and the state gets a ready-made lever of shame, which someone will use to make money. Varma blames incentives, not individual policemen. Take away the law, and the lever goes with it. {#threeseventy}

stories.start: In two thousand and three, uh, you know, I read news
stories.end: Who gets to define sanity and insanity? Where do you draw the line?
stories.caption: the German cannibal
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a case that tests the meaning of consent
stories.head: Dinner by mutual consent
body: In 2003, Amit Varma read about Armin Meiwes, a 42-year-old man in Rotenburg, Germany, whom his neighbours called normal. From the time he was eight, he had fantasised about eating a human being. {#eight}
He advertised for a well-built young man who wanted to be eaten. Bernd Brandes answered, saying he had always fantasised about being eaten, and consented at every stage, mostly on camera.

Brandes took twenty sleeping tablets and some schnapps. While he showered, Meiwes read a *Star Trek* novel. {#startrek} Then Meiwes killed him with a cleaver and ate the body over many days, with olive oil and garlic.

~ Cannibalism is not a crime in Germany; murder is. Is a man who consents to be eaten mentally ill, and if so, is the killer insane too? “Who gets to define sanity and insanity?” Varma asked. {073-S02}

quote.text: But there are many cases where it is not so clear cut and there is a continuum between sanity and insanity.

stories.postscript: On the olive oil and garlic, Varma wondered why there was no salt: “perhaps a human flesh has natural salt like bacon does.” {073-J06}

stories.start: And sugar is actually a great example. You know, we did an episode
stories.end: And the matter should just have been left to individuals to decide.
stories.caption: the sugar lobby
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lobby, some studies and a guideline
stories.head: Fat framed, sugar walks free
body: In the show’s episode on reversing his diabetes, Amit Varma had laid out how sugar is the root of many bad things. Some even call Alzheimer’s type three diabetes. {073-J17}

Yet for decades, especially in America, sugar was given a clean sheet and fat was demonised. The sugar lobby spent heavily on researchers from Harvard and elsewhere, whose influential studies used bad methodology and mistook correlation for causation.
In 1977 the top dietary body in the US issued guidelines saying sugar was fine and fat was evil. Look at a chart of the obesity epidemic, Varma said, and that is when it explodes. {#guidelines}
~ His conclusion was not to ban sugar. The state had stepped in believing it would do good. “But its knowledge was not good enough.” {073-S03}
stories.why: State guidance can be captured by a lobby and built on bad science, and because everyone follows it, the damage scales. Varma’s answer is not a ban but leaving the matter to individuals.

stories.start: Though I must point out that in all my years as a poker player
stories.end: things become far worse and everything goes south uh very quickly.
stories.caption: five years at the poker table
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the casino taught him
stories.head: Never a rupee on roulette
body: Amit Varma played poker professionally for five years and spent a lot of time in casinos. Not once in all that time did he play a game against the house, or put a single rupee on a roulette table. {#roulette}
It is a losing proposition, he said. In a sense, staying away was itself a gamble: he had weighed the probabilities.

The tables also showed him a darker side. He has seen gambling addiction destroy lives, as drug and alcohol addiction do, and when people close to him were caught by it, he tried to intervene and failed. {073-S05}
~ The state, he argued, can do nothing here: social problems have to be solved by society. “The state should know its limits. If the state tries to step in, things become far worse.”

quote.text: In the case of people close to me, I have tried to make interventions and I have failed because addiction is addiction.

quiz.q: In Bruce Yandle’s idea, which two figures both want alcohol banned, and why?
quiz.a: The Baptist, to signal virtue, and the bootlegger, to profit on the black market.

quiz.q: What share of people executed in advanced economies are later believed innocent, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: About 5 per cent, or one in twenty, despite the highest standards of evidence.

quiz.q: Where did police lure gay men in the racket Vikram Doctor told Amit Varma about?
quiz.a: To Matunga station, on the promise of coffee, before extorting money from them.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah call the greatest instrument for the emancipation and status of women?
quiz.a: Eight per cent GDP growth; anyone who cares about women should back it.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, does match-fixing happen in cricket?
quiz.a: Because betting is illegal, so the underworld runs it and nobody watches its money.

quiz.q: What happened in 1977 that Amit Varma links to America’s obesity epidemic?
quiz.a: The top US dietary body issued guidelines calling sugar fine and fat evil.
